  Elias Morrow had kept the light at Harrow Point for thirty-one years, and in
  all that time he had never once let it go dark.

  The automation crew was due on Thursday. They would install the sensors, the
  backup generators, the satellite uplink that would let someone in an office
  two hundred miles inland confirm, with a glance at a screen, that the lamp was
  turning. After that, Elias would be a line item in a budget review. A keeper
  without a keep.

  He climbed the hundred and twelve steps that evening as he always did, one
  hand on the cold iron rail. The wind came hard off the water, carrying salt
  and the smell of kelp rotting on the rocks below. At the top, he polished the
  lens. He did not need to. The crew had cleaned it on their survey visit, and
